source.title: EvoSLD: Automated Neural Scaling Law Discovery With Large Language Models
source.authors: Hao-Wei Lin; Hao-Tian Ye; Wen-Zheng Feng; Quzhe Huang; Yu-Jun Li; Hubert Lim; Zheng-Rui Li; Xiang-Yu Wang; Jian-Zhu Ma; Yi-Tao Liang; James Y. Zou

record.file_problem: Whole paper and appendices are present. The paper labels itself a preprint; no truncation or garbling that prevents reading the reported results.
record.tranche_reason: Tests extrapolation accuracy of scaling-law formulas on held-out data from multiple scaling-law tasks, using a benchmark and formulas rather than reproducing Kaplan et al. or Hoffmann et al.'s original measurement setup.
record.gate_note: The study tests law discovery and held-out extrapolation across benchmark tasks. It does not directly test the classical claim that held-out pretraining loss follows a power law in parameters, tokens, or compute, or measure a compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. The task-specific R² results below are extrapolation scores, not direct tests of a universal power-law form. Comparisons between agent implementations and other methods are not catalogued as separate scaling-law findings.
record.test_reason: The study fits task-specific scaling laws on seen runs and scores them on held-out runs with larger N, D, P or expert counts. Its human-baseline (literature) and agent-discovered laws give extrapolation R² that bears on V2 (modest extrapolation), V5 (SFT loss) and V6 (downstream Brier score versus compute). Most numbers compare the authors' agent with other agents, and the extrapolations are about 1.5–3.6×, not orders of magnitude.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that SLDAgent discovers laws that extrapolate more accurately than the human-derived laws on every task except parallel, where they tie. They also claim the laws are more principled (e.g. dimensionally consistent SFT form, bounded MoE asymptotics) and practically useful for hyperparameter choice and fine-tuning model selection. They acknowledge overfitting risk, possible training-time contamination, a limited benchmark and modest extrapolation splits.
record.recipe_differences: Uses an evolutionary symbolic-law discovery benchmark with seen/unseen dataset splits and task-specific formulas; it is not a direct replication of the original parameter/token/compute sweeps or compute-optimal allocation analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: Task and held-out split materially affect outcomes: u_shape remains a failure case, and the lr&bsz human baseline is below zero while the GPT-5 SLDAgent score is positive. The paper also reports variation across underlying LLMs and agent implementations, not extracted here as separate law-form findings.

fits_no_version.finding: Extrapolation accuracy depends strongly on the chosen law form and fitting routine on identical data. Examples: lr&bsz -0.076 (human) vs 0.604 (agent); the ablation gives -0.224 vs 0.194 with a fixed BFGS optimizer vs a co-optimized one.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The extrapolation accuracy of scaling-law fits depends on functional form and optimizer choice, not only on the data.

fits_no_version.finding: A loss law in lr, bsz, N and D fitted on smaller runs yields near-optimal hyperparameters for a 1B/100B-token run (loss 2.0776 vs optimum 2.0762).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Loss-surface laws over hyperparameters extrapolate the optimal learning rate and batch size to about 2× larger runs.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR), as given in the study metadata; the paper text labels the document a preprint.
record.problems: The paper explicitly notes possible training-time contamination from the literature, direct optimization on seen data without a dedicated validation set, and risk of overfitting. The held-out ranges are mostly modest compared with orders-of-magnitude extrapolation, and the u_shape task has negative R² even for SLDAgent.
record.rows_left_out: Table 3 provider-specific CLI-agent comparisons and Table 2 comparisons among other coding-agent systems are not included; they compare law-discovery workflows rather than add tests of the power-law or compute-optimal claims. No results are omitted due to the 60-row limit.

untested.parts: Power-law decline of held-out pretraining loss over several orders of magnitude is not measured.
Prediction for runs orders of magnitude larger is not tested; extrapolations are about 1.5–3.6×.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation is not tested.
Effects of depth, width or architecture shape at fixed parameter count are not tested.
Other modalities, repeated data (beyond the d_constrain fit) and transfer laws are not tested.
Downstream performance as a function of pretraining loss is not tested; only one adversarial U-shaped task is examined.

missing.what: RectifiedLaw (human SFT law) model-selection results: PearCorr 60.1/76.4/66.7 and RelAcc 100.0/44.0/78.3 on FLAN, Wikitext and Gigaword
Ablation of a fixed BFGS optimizer vs co-optimized fitting (o4-mini), e.g. lr&bsz -0.224 vs 0.194, average 0.775 vs 0.848
SLDAgent extrapolation R² with other LLMs per task (e.g. lr&bsz ranges from -0.871 to 0.611), showing that law quality varies

record.verdict_notes: The paper is primarily an agent benchmark, and most rows compare the authors' method with other methods. The human-baseline rows are the more neutral evidence on how well established laws extrapolate. Held-out splits are small-ratio extrapolations (≤~3.6×), so they cannot support V2's orders-of-magnitude part. The lr&bsz 'human' law is not from the literature. The u_shape task was deliberately chosen as adversarial.

versions.untested_parts: Does not directly test power-law decline of held-out pretraining loss against parameters, tokens, or compute when other variables are non-bottlenecks.
Tests held-out extrapolation on task-specific splits, generally about 1.5×–3.6× extrapolation or otherwise modest scale ranges; it does not test predictions for runs orders of magnitude larger.
The learning-rate/batch-size application does not test the compute-optimal split between parameter count and training tokens.
Does not compare depth, width, or architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Tests supervised fine-tuning loss against SFT dataset size. Does not test other modalities, repeated data, or transfer beyond the reported fine-tuning/model-selection setting.

Tests selecting fine-tuning models using small-subset SFT scaling-law predictions on three downstream datasets; does not test a general relationship between downstream performance and pretraining loss or model scale.
Although it compares different law formulations, it does not test whether exponents or compute-optimal allocations change with fitting choices, nor whether curves bend away from a single power law.

rows.note: The human baseline is the law from the original literature, refit on the seen split.

rows.operation_detail: Fits/evaluates SLDAgent-discovered scaling-law formula; R² averaged over five runs.

rows.subject: SLDBench d_constrain task
rows.operation_detail: Fits/evaluates SLDAgent-discovered scaling-law formula; R² averaged over five runs.
rows.note: Held-out points include the largest and second-largest values of model size or dataset size.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for V2 as written: R²=0.944 applies to the data-constrained held-out split, whose separation from seen scales is not established as orders of magnitude.

rows.subject: SLDBench lr&bsz task
rows.operation_detail: Fits/evaluates human-expert baseline scaling-law formula; R² averaged over five runs.
rows.note: The text identifies R² < 0 as worse-than-mean prediction; this is Expert B's law.
rows.check: The human baseline is an ad hoc law by a recruited master's student (Expert B), not a published law. The held-out set is a single (N,D) point, so R² mainly reflects the lr/bsz landscape plus any scale offset.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for V2 as written: Expert B's law scores R²=-0.076 across learning-rate and batch-size configurations at the held-out 1B-parameter, 100B-token setting.
source_check.problem: Failure of a joint scale-and-hyperparameter predictor at one held-out scale does not isolate failure of power-law extrapolation over orders of magnitude.

rows.subject: SLDBench lr&bsz task
rows.operation_detail: Fits/evaluates SLDAgent-discovered loss law; R² averaged over five runs.
rows.note: Held-out data use the largest model (1B parameters) and largest dataset (100B tokens).
rows.check: R² 0.604 is moderate. The agent law is log-quadratic in lr and bsz, not a pure power law. This is the study's own method.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for V2 as written: R²=0.604 evaluates the agent's log-quadratic loss predictor across hyperparameters at the held-out 1B-parameter, 100B-token setting.
source_check.problem: This score does not directly test power laws predicting loss over an orders-of-magnitude scale increase.

rows.subject: SLDBench u_shape task (aggregate over nine datasets)
rows.operation_detail: Fits/evaluates human baseline formula; R² averaged over five runs.
rows.note: The target is Brier score as a non-monotonic function of compute; the held-out set contains the final ascending phase.
rows.check: The target is downstream Brier score versus compute, which is V6, not V2's pretraining loss. The value -1.000 may be clipped to [-1,1].

rows.subject: SLDBench u_shape task (aggregate over nine datasets)
rows.operation_detail: Fits/evaluates SLDAgent-discovered formula; R² averaged over five runs.
rows.note: The paper describes u_shape as a primary outlier and the task as particularly challenging.
rows.check: Downstream Brier score versus compute belongs to V6. R² -0.305 is worse than predicting the mean.

rows.subject: SLDAgentLaw
rows.operation_detail: Uses an SFT scaling law fitted on 6.25% of the full dataset to select among 14 candidate models; reports Pearson correlation.
rows.measure: Pearson correlation coefficient (percent) for ranking model performance
rows.note: The reported task is selecting the model with the best full-data fine-tuning performance.
rows.check: This predicts full-data fine-tuning performance from an SFT law fitted on 6.25% of the data, which is fine-tuning scaling (V5). It is not downstream-versus-pretraining-scale (V6). It is also the study's own law compared with selection baselines.

rows.subject: 1B-parameter LLM in the lr&bsz extrapolation setting
rows.operation_detail: Trains at the nearest available grid point to the hyperparameters analytically predicted by the SLDAgent law.

conditions.value: Nearest grid point to predicted optimum lr = 1.77 × 10−3, bsz = 402

rows.measure: Actual validation loss at the nearest grid point, compared with true optimal validation loss
rows.note: The paper describes this as near-optimal performance in a setting at least twice as large as all observed experiments; this is not a test of parameter/token allocation.

relationships.condition: SFT loss versus fine-tuning data size, 42 model/dataset pairs (2× extrapolation) and 6.25%-subset model selection on FLAN, Wikitext and Gigaword

relationships.display_finding: Fine-tuning laws achieved held-out R² of 0.957–0.993 and ranked 14 models with reported Pearson values of 83.6–94.8 and RelAcc of 100.

relationships.condition: U-shaped downstream Brier score versus compute on nine easy-question datasets (final ascending phase held out)
